rules.title: 2023 TV/Theatrical: employment-based digital replicas
rules.status: in force as modified by 2026 agreement (see sag-aftra-tvt-2026)
rules.applies_when: a covered production creates or uses a digital replica of a performer it employs (voice or likeness in material the performer did not actually perform)
requires: Give the performer at least 48 hours' notice of replica-creation services (or notice at engagement if engaged less than 48 hours ahead).
Obtain informed consent that is clear and conspicuous, separately signed or initialed, and includes a reasonably specific description of the intended use; it cannot be buried in boilerplate.
Consent is project-specific; use in another picture needs fresh consent and separately bargained pay (day-performer rate as floor).
Pay for replica use in the same picture based on the estimated in-person days the replica scenes would have required, plus residuals where applicable.
For a deceased performer, obtain consent from the estate or rights holder.
evidence: Signed/initialed digital replica consent rider with the use description, linked to the shot/asset IDs it covers
Notice timestamp showing 48-hour notice for scan/capture sessions
Mapping of replica-generated shots to the consented project and use description
Payment calculation records for replica-generated scenes
workflow_signals: face-swap / identity / IP-adapter-face / InstantID / PuLID nodes fed with a real performer's images
LoRA trained on a specific performer's scans or footage
voice-clone TTS or speech-to-speech nodes using a performer's recordings
lip-sync / dialogue-replacement nodes on a performer's face
rules.source_title: Digital Replicas 101: What You Need to Know About the 2023 TV/Theatrical Contracts
rules.notes: Union explainer is undated. The 2026 TV/Theatrical agreement (effective 2026-07-01) substantially revises these replica terms; check the 2026 MOA text before relying on the 2023 mechanics. Not checked here: the full 2023 contract text, the background-performer terms, and the exact compensation formulas.

rules.title: 2023 TV/Theatrical: independently created replicas and digital alteration
rules.status: in force as modified by 2026 agreement
rules.applies_when: a replica of a performer is made without an employment arrangement (e.g. from existing footage) and gives the impression it is that performer, or a performer's recorded performance is digitally altered beyond routine post
requires: Obtain explicit, signed or initialed consent with a reasonably specific use description, unless the content stays substantially as performed or scripted.
For a deceased performer, get consent from the estate, or from the union if no estate can be found.
Make pension and health contributions for independently created replicas.
Routine post changes (cosmetics, wardrobe, continuity, pitch, timing, VFX filters, ratings or S&P edits, foreign-language lip adjustments) do not require consent.
evidence: Classification of each AI alteration as routine post (exempt) or beyond script/performance (consent needed)
Source-material provenance for any replica built from existing footage
Consent document or estate/union authorization
workflow_signals: face/identity nodes using archival or library footage of a real performer
inpainting or video-to-video that changes a performer's dialogue, expression or actions
de-aging or relighting nodes (likely routine post, but log them)
rules.source_title: Artificial Intelligence Terms of SAG-AFTRA TV/Theatrical Contract (Loeb & Loeb)
rules.notes: This is a law-firm summary of the 2023 tentative agreement, not the contract text. The First Amendment carve-outs (comment, parody, docudrama, biography) apply to independently created replicas. The exempt-alteration list comes from the SAG-AFTRA explainer PDF.

rules.title: 2023 TV/Theatrical: synthetic performers
rules.applies_when: a covered production uses a fully AI-generated, realistic human character in place of a human performer
requires: Notify the union and give it an opportunity to bargain in good faith over consideration when a synthetic performer replaces a human role.
If a synthetic performer's principal facial feature (eyes, nose, ears, mouth) is recognizable as a specific real performer, get that performer's consent and bargain.
Non-human characters are outside this rule.
evidence: Record of union notice for synthetic human characters
Prompt/reference-image log showing no real performer's features were used to generate the character (or consent if they were)
workflow_signals: text-to-image/video generating photoreal human characters with no performer source
reference images or LoRAs of real people used in character generation
rules.source_title: Artificial Intelligence Terms of SAG-AFTRA TV/Theatrical Contract (Loeb & Loeb)
rules.notes: Law-firm summary. See sag-aftra-tvt-2026 for the stricter 2026 standard.

rules.title: 2026 TV/Theatrical Agreement AI terms
rules.applies_when: a SAG-AFTRA-covered film/TV production scans performers, uses digital replicas (including of minors), or uses synthetic performers in human roles
requires: Have an articulable business reason before scanning a performer to create a digital replica.
Do not use a performer's digital replica to replace them during a strike.
Apply new protections for replicas of minors (details not verified).
Do not use a synthetic performer in a human role unless it adds significant additional value compared with both a union performer and that performer's digital replica.
Be prepared for union bargaining over planned synthetic use, with arbitration and damages not capped at what a human performer would have earned.
Follow the revised consent, compensation, residual, security and transfer rules for replica assets (summarized, not verified in detail).
evidence: Documented business justification for each scan session
Replica asset register: who holds it, access controls, transfers
Synthetic-performer value justification memo per role
Flags for minors' likeness in any replica workflow
workflow_signals: photogrammetry / Gaussian-splat / volumetric capture of performers
replica LoRAs or identity embeddings stored as reusable assets
synthetic human characters in speaking or featured roles
any identity node whose source person is a minor
rules.human_in_loop: Indirect: the synthetic-performer standard favors human performance, so keep records of which roles humans performed.
rules.source_title: SAG-AFTRA Members Ratify New Contract With Over 91% Approval (TheWrap)
rules.notes: Press coverage only (TheWrap 2026-06-04; Shoot 2026-05-12; LA Mag 2026-06-05 gives term 2026-07-01 to 2030-06-30). The full MOA and 18-page union summary were not fetched. The scanning, strike and minors items come from Shoot/TheWrap deal-details coverage. Jackson Lewis (2026-07-22) says the deal also covers security and transfer of replica assets.

rules.title: 2025 Commercials Contracts (incl. Audio) AI terms
rules.applies_when: a union commercial creates or uses a performer's digital replica, uses synthetic performers, or uses performer data
requires: Give 48 hours' notice before creating or using a digital replica (less if the performer was engaged within 48 hours).

Obtain written informed consent via a Digital Replica Rider or separate signed writing, with a reasonably specific description of use; new consent is needed for uses outside that description, altered physical traits or nudity.
Pay at least 1.5x scale session fee per commercial generated with a replica, plus use and holding fees as if the performer had worked in person.
Destroy the replica after the Maximum Period of Use unless consent to retain is obtained; limit access and use commercially reasonable security.
Do not use performer data to train AI without union consent.
For synthetic performers, pay pension and health amounts set by the contract (or negotiated, for all-synthetic spots); synthetic use is acceptable if cost saving is not the primary motive.
Traditional VFX/CGI/mocap tools that incorporate AI remain allowed for past-practice purposes.
evidence: Digital Replica Rider per performer per spot, with use description
MPU tracking and replica destruction/retention records
Access log for stored replica assets (LoRAs, voice models, scans)
Statement that performer footage was not used for model training, or union consent
Synthetic-performer usage report for P&H calculation
workflow_signals: performer identity LoRA or voice model reused across spots
training/fine-tuning nodes fed with talent footage
synthetic on-camera or voice characters in a union spot
rules.source_title: 2025 Commercials Contracts (SAG-AFTRA)
rules.notes: The union page's FAQ is a summary. Details are corroborated by DLA Piper (2025-04-28) and Davis+Gilbert (2025-06-11), and the effective date is from Davis+Gilbert. Check the MOA for exact definitions.

rules.title: 2025 Interactive Media Agreement AI terms
rules.applies_when: a covered game uses vocal or visual digital replicas of performers, or independently created replicas (including prompting a model with a performer's name)
requires: Obtain clear and conspicuous written consent (separate document or specifically signed rider) with a reasonably specific use description.
Disclose whether the replica will be used for real-time generation and whether sensitive content (e.g. profanity, slurs) may be generated.
Generally obtain consent at the time of use rather than at hiring for future games.
Pay for vocal replica use by lines generated (about 10 words per line).
Provide a usage report within 90 days of release naming characters that used replicas and how pay was computed.
evidence: Consent rider with real-time and sensitive-content disclosures
Generated-line counts per performer replica
90-day usage report
workflow_signals: voice-clone TTS producing new dialogue
prompts naming a real performer
real-time generation pipelines
rules.source_title: Inside the New SAG-AFTRA Interactive Media Agreement (Frankfurt Kurnit)
rules.notes: Law-firm summary. The ratification announcement date of 2025-07-09 (95% approval) is from FKKS (2025-07-11). Traditional animation AI, noise reduction and rigging are excluded. Relevant to a commercial/film studio only for game cinematics or interactive work.

rules.title: WGA MBA AI provisions (2023, carried into 2026)
rules.applies_when: AI-generated text is given to a covered writer, or a writer uses AI, or literary material is licensed for AI training
requires: AI is not a writer, and AI-generated text is not literary material or source material for credit and pay purposes.
The company must tell the writer if material it provides was AI-generated or contains AI-generated content.
The company cannot require a writer to use AI; a writer may use AI only with company consent and in line with company policy.
2026 additions (reported): regular labor-management meetings on GenAI use, and written notice to the WGA when literary material is licensed to train public-facing commercial AI systems.
evidence: Record of which scripts, treatments or prompts handed to writers were AI-generated, and the disclosure given
Company AI-use policy and any consent given to writers
Note: prompt text used in image/video workflows is not literary material under the MBA, but keep authorship records for scripts
workflow_signals: LLM nodes generating scripts, dialogue or story beats
AI-generated text fed into a covered writer's process
rules.human_in_loop: Credit and pay attach only to human writers, so keep records of who wrote what.
rules.source_title: Know Your Rights: Artificial Intelligence (WGA)
rules.notes: The 2026 MBA was ratified 2026-04-24 with 90.38% approval (WGA press release). The 2026 AI additions are from Jackson Lewis (2026-07-22), not the MBA text; the WGA 2026 summary was not fetched. Mostly relevant to writing, not pixels.

rules.title: DGA Basic Agreement AI terms (2023 and 2026)
rules.status: in force (2026 agreement ratified 2026-06-26, four-year term)
rules.applies_when: generative AI is used on creative elements of a DGA-covered production
requires: Generative AI is not a person, and DGA members' duties cannot be assigned to it (2023).
Do not use GenAI on creative elements without consulting the director; the director's input must be considered in good faith. This is consultation, not approval (2023).
2026: AI-generated footage falls under the director's creative control; new transparency duties on GenAI use and on licensing covered work for training (reported).
evidence: Record that the director was consulted, and signed off where 2026 terms require, on each AI-generated shot or element
Director/approver identity attached to the shot's workflow history
workflow_signals: any generative node producing final-pixel shots on a DGA show
training or fine-tuning on production footage
rules.human_in_loop: Directly relevant: this is the clearest contractual 'human creative control' duty in US film/TV. Capturing the director or approver per AI shot is the natural evidence.
rules.source_title: DGA Board Recommends Ratification of New Contract
rules.notes: The DGA release gives only summary terms (renewed 2023 safeguards, director control over AI footage, skills program). The 2023 terms are from TheWrap (2023-06-07). The 2026 transparency/training detail is from Jackson Lewis (2026-07-22). Ratification: DGA press release 2026-06-26, no vote count. Effective date 2026-07-01 is inferred from the prior term ending 2026-06-30 and was not stated in a fetched 2026 source.

rules.authority: Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences
rules.title: 99th Oscars eligibility rules on generative AI
rules.status: in force for films released 2026-01-01 to 2026-12-31
rules.applies_when: a film using generative AI is submitted for Academy Awards
requires: Acting nominations: performances must be by consenting humans in billed roles.
Screenplays must be human-authored.
Human authorship must be present in films that use GenAI.
The Academy may request information about GenAI use and the human authorship involved.
evidence: Per-shot record of GenAI use and the human contributions (direction, selection, compositing, paint)
Performer consent records for any AI-modified performance
workflow_signals: feature-film deliverables containing generative shots
AI-modified performances
rules.human_in_loop: Yes. This is an awards-eligibility rule, not law, but it explicitly lets the Academy ask for proof of human authorship.
rules.source_title: Awards Rules and Campaign Promotional Regulations Approved for 99th Oscars
rules.notes: Private awards rule, not a legal obligation.

rules.title: Copyright and AI, Part 2: Copyrightability
rules.applies_when: a studio wants copyright protection in content that contains AI-generated material
requires: Only human authorship is protected; purely AI-generated material is not.
Prompts alone, including revised and resubmitted prompts, do not currently give enough control to make the user an author.
Human expressive inputs that remain perceptible in the output (e.g. an artist's own drawing, plate or model) stay protected.
Creative selection, coordination, arrangement or modification of AI output can be protected, case by case.
AI used as an assistive tool (e.g. de-aging, color correction, crowd removal) does not undermine protection of the human work.
No new legislation or sui generis right is recommended.
evidence: Human-made inputs per shot: plates, paintovers, 3D layouts, sketches, control maps, with author IDs
Record of human modifications after generation (comp, paint, roto, grading) with before/after versions
Selection and arrangement decisions (which takes were chosen and why, the edit)
Prompt and seed history, which shows process but is not by itself evidence of authorship
workflow_signals: ControlNet/depth/pose/img2img nodes driven by human-made inputs
pure text-to-image/video with no human input image
post-generation comp/paint steps in Nuke or similar
rules.human_in_loop: Central. Protection depends on the human's expressive contribution, so the workflow history should separate human inputs and edits from model output.
rules.source_title: Copyright and Artificial Intelligence, Part 2: Copyrightability
rules.notes: This is agency guidance; courts decide case by case. Related: Part 3 on training was released as a pre-publication version on 2025-05-09 and concludes fair use is case by case. Its final status is uncertain after the Register's removal (Jenner). Allen v. Perlmutter (D. Colo. 1:24-cv-2665), a test of a heavily iterated Midjourney image, was still pending as of a 2026-03-30 tracker; no ruling was found.

rules.title: Registration guidance for works containing AI-generated material
rules.applies_when: a studio registers a work (film, spot, artwork) containing more than de minimis AI-generated material
requires: Disclose AI-generated content in the application and briefly describe the human author's contribution.
Use the Standard Application, and exclude more-than-de-minimis AI material under Limitation of Claim (Material Excluded).
Do not list an AI tool or its vendor as an author.
Correct pending applications, or file a supplementary registration for issued ones, if AI material was not disclosed.
Failure to disclose risks cancellation, or the registration being disregarded in litigation if inaccuracy was knowing.
evidence: Inventory of AI-generated portions per work, enough to write the Material Excluded statement
Description of human-authored contributions per work
workflow_signals: any final deliverable containing generative output that the studio intends to register
rules.human_in_loop: Yes. The application must state the human contribution, so the workflow history should support that statement.
rules.source_title: Copyright Registration Guidance: Works Containing Material Generated by Artificial Intelligence (88 FR, 2023-05321)
rules.notes: Reaffirmed in Part 2 (2025).

rules.authority: U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit; U.S. Supreme Court (cert. denied)
rules.title: Thaler v. Perlmutter
rules.applies_when: a work is claimed with an AI system as author or with no human authorial contribution
requires: The Copyright Act requires a human author in the first instance; a machine cannot be the author.
evidence: Identify human authors for every protected deliverable
workflow_signals: fully autonomous generation with no human creative input
rules.human_in_loop: Sets the floor (zero human input means no protection) but does not decide how much human involvement is enough.
rules.source_title: Supreme Court Denies Certiorari in Thaler v. Perlmutter (Baker Donelson)
rules.notes: D.C. Cir. No. 23-5233, decided 2025-03-18; S. Ct. No. 25-449, cert denied 2026-03-02 (SCOTUSblog). The court opinion PDF was not fetched directly.

rules.authority: EU (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, AI Act), as amended by Reg. (EU) 2026/1744
rules.title: AI Act Art. 50(2): machine-readable marking of synthetic output
rules.status: in force from 2026-08-02; systems already on the market before then have until 2026-12-02
rules.applies_when: the studio is a provider of a generative AI system (built, or substantially modified, its own model/system and places it on the market or puts it into service) whose synthetic audio, image, video or text reaches the EU
requires: Mark outputs in a machine-readable format so they are detectable as AI-generated or manipulated.
Marking must be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as technically feasible, considering the state of the art.
Exempt: systems that only assist standard editing or do not substantially alter the input or its meaning.
evidence: Whether the studio is acting as a provider (own fine-tuned model or tool offered to others) or only as a deployer of third-party tools
Marking method applied per output (signed metadata / C2PA manifest, watermark), and verification that it survives the delivery pipeline
Vendor contract terms guaranteeing marking by upstream model providers
workflow_signals: studio-trained or fine-tuned models/LoRAs offered as a service or tool
output distributed in the EU
metadata-stripping steps (re-encode, EXR/ProRes conversion) that could remove marks
rules.human_in_loop: None. Art. 50 is about marking and disclosure, not human oversight.
rules.source_title: Article 50: Transparency obligations for providers and deployers of certain AI systems (AI Act Service Desk)
rules.notes: Source date is the date of the consolidated text shown. The 2026-12-02 grace period for pre-existing systems comes from the Digital Omnibus on AI (Reg. (EU) 2026/1744, OJ 2026-07-24, per Cuatrecasas). The watermark-detection interoperability measure applies from 2027-02-02 under the Code (Freshfields). Whether a studio running open models in ComfyUI internally is a 'provider' is a legal judgment; DLA Piper (2026-07-16) notes that building or substantially modifying generative tools can make a studio a provider. Fines for Art. 50 breaches: up to EUR 15m or 3% of turnover (Art. 99(4), per DLA Piper).

rules.title: AI Act Art. 50(4): deepfake disclosure by deployers
rules.applies_when: a studio uses an AI system to generate or manipulate image, audio or video that resembles real people, objects, places or events and could falsely appear authentic, and the content is shown in the EU
requires: Disclose that the content is artificially generated or manipulated, clearly and distinguishably, at the latest at first exposure, and accessibly.

For evidently artistic, creative, satirical or fictional works, the duty is limited to disclosing the existence of such content in a way that does not hamper display or enjoyment (e.g. credits or notes, per commentary).
The Commission reads the creative exception strictly; where content mixes informative and creative elements, the informative character prevails (relevant to ads making factual claims).
Content depicting impossible creatures or physics-defying scenes is not a deepfake (per Code commentary).
evidence: Per-deliverable flag: contains realistic AI-generated/manipulated depiction of real-seeming people, places or events (Y/N)
Disclosure method and placement used (on-screen icon, credits, spoken disclaimer) and the territories where it was shown
Rationale if the creative-work lighter regime was relied on
workflow_signals: photoreal people/places generated or manipulated
face-swap, lip-sync, voice clone
output distributed in EU
advertising making factual product claims
rules.human_in_loop: No human-in-the-loop proof is required for audiovisual content. The human review / editorial responsibility exemption in Art. 50(4) applies only to AI-generated text published to inform the public.
rules.source_title: Article 50 (AI Act Service Desk)
rules.notes: Commission Art. 50 guidelines published 2026-07-20 (Stephenson Harwood, 2026-08-03). The deepfake definition is in Art. 3(60) and was paraphrased via DLA Piper rather than fetched. National laws may add requirements (e.g. French Penal Code Art. 226-8, per DLA Piper).

rules.title: Code of Practice on Transparency (marking and labelling) of AI-generated content
rules.applies_when: a provider or deployer wants a recognized way to show Art. 50(2)/(4) compliance
requires: Providers: use digitally signed, time-stamped, tamper-evident metadata plus imperceptible watermarking (multi-layer where one technique is insufficient); fingerprinting/logging is optional.
Providers: preserve existing metadata where feasible, bar users from stripping marks in terms of service, offer a free public detection tool, and implement detection interoperability by 2027-02-02.

Deployers: label deepfakes using the EU icon (fully generated / AI-modified / basic) or an equivalent label, recognizable without interaction at first exposure; use spoken disclaimers for audio-only content.
Deployers: adopt proportionate internal processes, awareness and review mechanisms for labelling.
evidence: Labelling SOP and record of label/icon applied per deliverable
Provenance metadata retained through delivery
Training/awareness records for staff who approve labelling
workflow_signals: deliverables for EU distribution
export steps that may strip metadata
rules.human_in_loop: Only for text: deployers relying on the editorial exemption must name the person with editorial responsibility and document review processes, though not each individual review.
rules.source_title: Commission publishes Code of Practice on marking and labelling AI-generated content
rules.notes: Measure details come from Freshfields and IPTC summaries; the Code text itself was not read. Adherence is voluntary and not conclusive evidence of compliance. According to IPTC, the Code does not name C2PA and refers only to 'relevant standards'; IPTC's view that C2PA is the only technology meeting the criteria is its own commentary.

rules.title: AI Act Art. 14: human oversight (high-risk systems only)
rules.status: Annex III high-risk obligations deferred to 2027-12-02 (Annex I to 2028-08-02) by Digital Omnibus
rules.applies_when: only when the AI system is high-risk (Annex I products or Annex III uses such as biometrics, employment, education, law enforcement, essential services, justice/elections); creative content generation is not an Annex III area
requires: Providers design high-risk systems so natural persons can understand, monitor, override and stop them; deployers apply those measures.
Does not apply to generative tools used for film, TV or advertising content unless used in a listed high-risk context (e.g. AI used to screen or hire performers would be employment-area high-risk).
evidence: Classification memo showing the creative pipeline is not a high-risk use
Separate review if AI is used in casting/hiring decisions (employment area)
workflow_signals: AI used to rank or screen talent or crew (employment) - out of scope for pixel workflows
rules.human_in_loop: This is the AI Act's human-in-the-loop article, but it applies only to high-risk systems. There is no EU legal requirement to prove a human was in the loop for an AI-generated creative shot.
rules.source_title: Article 14: Human oversight (AI Act Service Desk)
rules.notes: The Annex III list was checked at https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/annex-3. Deferral dates are from Cuatrecasas (2026-07-24). Separately, amended Art. 4 (AI literacy) still requires providers/deployers to take measures for staff AI literacy.

rules.authority: Court of Justice of the EU
rules.title: Originality = author's own intellectual creation (Infopaq C-5/08; Painer C-145/10)
rules.applies_when: a studio claims copyright in AI-assisted content in an EU member state
requires: A work is protected only if it is the author's own intellectual creation reflecting their personality through free and creative choices (Painer: framing, angle, lighting and similar choices for photos).
Choices dictated by technical constraints that leave no room for creativity do not qualify (Football Dataco, per commentary).
evidence: Records of human creative choices visible in the final frame: composition, framing, lighting, layout, paintovers, edit decisions
Link between those choices and the output (e.g. control images, masks, comp scripts)
workflow_signals: human-authored control inputs (layout, depth, pose, sketch)
manual comp/paint/grade after generation
pure prompt-only generation (weak)
rules.human_in_loop: Central for protectability (not for legality). Evidence of free and creative human choices is what supports protection.
rules.source_title: CJEU C-145/10 Painer, Judgment of 1 December 2011 (FRA case-law reference)
rules.notes: Infopaq (C-5/08, 16 July 2009) was not fetched from a primary source (BAILII was blocked, IPPT paywalled); the date is from search results and commentary. The CJEU has not ruled on AI-generated outputs. C-250/25 Like Company v Google (referred 2025-04-03) concerns training and outputs reproducing press content, not output protectability, and a ruling is not expected before 2027.

rules.title: AG Munich: AI-generated logos not protected
rules.applies_when: a studio relies on prompting (even long or iterated prompts) to claim copyright in AI output in Germany
requires: AI output can be protected only if human input (carefully designed prompts, settings, selective revision) shapes the result in an objectively identifiable way, with the creative prompt elements dominating the output.
Merely selecting from AI options or iterating technical adjustments is not sufficient; a 1,700-character prompt was still too abstract, and effort alone does not count.
evidence: Prompt history together with evidence that specific human choices determine specific visual features
Human edits beyond selection
workflow_signals: prompt-only generation with cherry-picking
iterative seed/parameter tweaking without human-made inputs
rules.human_in_loop: Yes for protectability. The court examined the prompts and iteration process in detail, so keeping that history matters, but it may show insufficient control.
rules.source_title: CMS AI & copyright case tracker: Germany, AI-generated logos
rules.notes: Secondary source (CMS tracker); case number not stated. A lower-court ruling with limited precedential weight. Jurisdiction is Germany (EU member state).

rules.authority: Mestsky soud v Praze (Prague Municipal Court), Czech Republic
rules.title: Prague Municipal Court 10 C 13/2023: AI image not a work
rules.applies_when: a claimant asserts authorship of a text-to-image output in Czechia
requires: Only a natural person can be an author; an AI-generated image that is not the result of a person's creative activity is not a work.
A prompt is at most an idea or theme and is not protected.
The claimant also failed to prove that his prompt produced the image, offering only his own statement.
evidence: Contemporaneous, verifiable records linking prompt, settings and output (the claimant lost partly for lack of such proof)
workflow_signals: prompt-only text-to-image deliverables
rules.human_in_loop: Shows evidentiary risk: without a verifiable generation record, even authorship of the prompt could not be proven.
rules.source_title: IRIS Merlin (European Audiovisual Observatory) report on 10 C 13/2023
rules.notes: Decision dated 11 October; the year was not shown in the fetched text (commonly reported as 2023, with Bird & Bird's commentary in 2024). Facts are from Bird & Bird.

rules.authority: Landgericht Muenchen I (Regional Court Munich I), Germany
rules.title: GEMA v OpenAI (42 O 14139/24)
rules.applies_when: a model memorizes and reproduces protected works in outputs
requires: Memorization of works in model parameters is reproduction; outputs reproducing lyrics infringed reproduction and making-available rights.
The EU TDM exception does not cover memorizing whole works.
The model provider, not the user, was held responsible for infringing outputs.
evidence: Model/checkpoint identity and provenance per shot (which provider is responsible)
Output similarity checks against known third-party IP for final deliverables
workflow_signals: outputs that closely resemble existing copyrighted characters, artwork or footage
unknown-provenance community checkpoints/LoRAs
rules.source_title: GEMA v OpenAI: Regional Court of Munich I, 11 November 2025 (Taylor Wessing)
rules.notes: Concerns text lyrics and an LLM provider; extending it to image/video models is untested. It does not bear on human-in-the-loop evidence.

rules.authority: Hanseatisches Oberlandesgericht Hamburg (Higher Regional Court), Germany
rules.title: Kneschke v LAION (5 U 104/24)
rules.status: appeal decided; further appeal to BGH allowed
rules.applies_when: training datasets are built from scraped images (relevant if a studio builds training sets for LoRAs or fine-tunes)
requires: A non-commercial research organisation may rely on the scientific-research TDM exception (s60d UrhG).
A natural-language reservation in website terms was not machine-readable in 2021 and so not a valid opt-out; the court treated this as time-dependent.
evidence: Training-data provenance and licence/opt-out checks for any studio-trained LoRA or fine-tune
workflow_signals: LoRA / fine-tune training nodes
dataset scraping
rules.source_title: Higher Regional Court Hamburg confirms AI training was permitted (Bird & Bird)
rules.notes: Judgment date and reference (10 Dec 2025, 5 U 104/24) are from search-result titles (Technology's Legal Edge); the Bird & Bird page did not state them. A commercial studio would not benefit from the research exception.

rules.title: CDPA s9(3) computer-generated works and the 2026 Copyright and AI report
rules.status: in force; government proposes removal (no legislation yet)
rules.applies_when: a work is generated by computer with no human author and protection is claimed in the UK
requires: The author of a computer-generated work is the person who made the arrangements necessary for its creation; protection lasts 50 years and carries no moral rights.
The March 2026 government report proposes removing s9(3) protection after further monitoring, while AI-assisted human works remain protected.
The broad TDM exception with opt-out is no longer the preferred option; there are no concrete labelling or transparency proposals.
evidence: Who made the arrangements (producer/operator) for each generated asset, in case s9(3) is relied on
Human-authorship records, which are safer given the proposed repeal
workflow_signals: UK-produced or UK-exploited deliverables containing autonomous generation

corrections: The EU does not legally require proof that a human was in the loop for an AI-generated shot. AI Act Art. 14 (human oversight) applies only to high-risk AI systems (Annex I products and Annex III areas such as biometrics, employment, education, law enforcement and justice). Creative content generation is not in Annex III, and Annex III obligations are now deferred to 2027-12-02. What applies to creative work is Art. 50 transparency: providers mark output in machine-readable form, and deployers disclose deepfakes (lighter duty for evidently artistic or fictional works). Art. 50's human-review/editorial-responsibility exemption covers only AI-generated text on matters of public interest, not images or video.

Human involvement matters in the EU and elsewhere for copyright protectability, not for legality. Under the CJEU originality test (free and creative choices), the Czech 10 C 13/2023 ruling and the AG Munich February 2026 logos ruling, little or no human creative input means no copyright. Records of human creative choices are therefore valuable evidence, but they are not a regulatory compliance requirement.

In US film and TV, the closest thing to a 'human in the loop' duty is contractual: DGA terms (AI is not a person; consult the director, and under the 2026 deal AI footage falls under the director's creative control), SAG-AFTRA consent rules, and the Academy's 99th Oscars rule that human authorship be present, which lets the Academy request details. The US Copyright Office registration guidance requires disclosing AI material and describing the human contribution.

MPAA was renamed the Motion Picture Association (MPA) on 2019-09-18. The MPA is a trade association. It has no binding AI production rules; its AI output is policy advocacy (copyright and fair use, support for the NO FAKES Act). CARA/film ratings do not regulate AI use (no AI provision was found, though the rating rules PDF was not read).
The DGA's 2023 AI term requires consultation with the director, not the director's approval.

California SB 942 (AI Transparency Act) binds large GenAI providers (over 1M monthly users), not studios directly. Its operative date moved from 2026-01-01 to 2026-08-02 under AB 853. Studios are affected as licensees, who must not disable latent disclosures.

EU AI Act Art. 50(2) marking falls on providers of generative systems (model and tool vendors), not on every studio that uses them. A studio that builds or substantially modifies its own generative system may become a provider. Systems already on the market before 2026-08-02 have until 2026-12-02 under the Digital Omnibus (Reg. (EU) 2026/1744). Deployer deepfake disclosure under Art. 50(4) applied from 2026-08-02 without delay.

The EU Code of Practice on transparency of AI-generated content (final 2026-06-10) is voluntary and, per IPTC, does not name C2PA. It calls for signed, time-stamped metadata plus watermarking under 'relevant standards'.

Thaler v. Perlmutter settles only that an AI cannot be the author when there is no human contribution. It does not set how much human input is enough; that question is open (Allen v. Perlmutter was still pending when last checked).
The NO FAKES Act is not law (reintroduced 2026-05-20; committee stage). The TAKE IT DOWN Act is in force but limited to nonconsensual intimate imagery.

US Copyright Office Part 2 says AI used as an assistive tool (e.g. de-aging, color correction, crowd removal) does not undermine protection. Routine VFX uses of AI are treated differently from prompt-only generation, as are SAG-AFTRA's exempt post-production alterations.
